name: Repository Code Readability & Structural Refactorer
sprintRole: Refactor bloated or tangled source code into cohesive, obvious ownership boundaries that humans and agents can understand and edit safely without behavior drift
useWhen: Source code has become difficult to navigate or change because files, functions, classes, modules, branches, responsibilities, naming, duplication, or indirection have grown beyond clear human/agent editability, even when tests still pass.
inspectFirst: Repository governance and code map; target source and tests; public APIs, schemas, serialization and artifact contracts; call/import graph and ownership boundaries; generated-code/source ownership; file/function/class size and complexity signals when available; duplication and dead-code evidence; recent change hotspots and regressions; formatter/linter/type/build/test conventions.
expectedOutput: A behavior-preserving readability refactor with a structural-debt ledger, smaller and clearer ownership surfaces, characterization/regression tests where needed, measured or evidence-backed before/after editability improvements, no hand-edited generated output, and exact validation/integration proof.
nextStep: Refactor the highest-impact evidenced readability hotspot now, run its characterization/regression and repository gates, perform a deliberate second pass for new indirection or leftover structural debt, then integrate the exact green bounded slice or name the precise blocker.
proofGate: Externally observable behavior and owned contracts remain unchanged unless explicitly in scope; each moved responsibility has one obvious owner; duplicate/dead/tangled code is removed only with evidence; generated surfaces are changed through their canonical source/generator; the candidate does not replace a monolith with a maze of trivial abstractions; representative maintenance paths are easier to locate and edit; targeted and impacted regressions pass; and a deliberate second pass finds no practical high-impact readability repair remaining in owned scope.
copyContent:
REFACTOR THE REPOSITORY CODE FOR HUMAN AND AGENT READABILITY. DO NOT TURN THIS INTO COSMETIC FORMATTING, A REWRITE FOR ITS OWN SAKE, OR A LINE-COUNT CONTEST.

Repo: xyz_repo_or_path
Target scope or hotspot: xyz_scope_or_resolve_from_evidence
Known readability pain, if any: xyz_readability_problem
Forbidden behavior changes: xyz_forbidden_behavior_or_resolve_from_repo

MISSION
Make the owned source code easier for a fresh human or agent to navigate, understand, modify, review, and test while preserving externally observable behavior and repository contracts unless a behavior change is explicitly in scope. Treat passing tests as necessary but not sufficient: a green change that needlessly creates a god file, giant function, mixed responsibility, duplicate logic, or an abstraction maze has not solved the editability problem.

1. REFRESH AND MAP THE REAL OWNER
- Refresh current repository/default-branch truth and overlapping work before mutation. Preserve dirty or separately owned work.
- Read repository governance, code maps, target source/tests, public APIs, schemas, serializers, artifact contracts, and generated-code ownership.
- Trace practical callers/imports and identify where a maintainer would currently change each responsibility. Do not refactor from file size alone.

2. BUILD A STRUCTURAL-DEBT LEDGER
For each concrete hotspot classify it as KEEP, EXTRACT, SPLIT, RENAME, DEDUPLICATE, DELETE-DEAD, MOVE-TO-CANONICAL-OWNER, GENERATED-SOURCE-REPAIR, or DEFER. Support the disposition with code/test/history/tool evidence. Useful signals include:
- one file/class/function owning unrelated responsibilities;
- deep nesting or branch logic that obscures the main path;
- duplicated conditions, transformations, constants, or error handling;
- names/comments that hide domain intent or disagree with behavior;
- broad mutable state, hidden coupling, circular or surprising imports;
- one small change requiring edits across many unrelated places;
- repeated agent/human difficulty finding the correct owner;
- dead compatibility paths or wrappers with no remaining consumer;
- hand-edited generated output instead of its canonical generator/source.
Line counts, cyclomatic complexity, churn, fan-in/fan-out, or duplication metrics may prioritize inspection when available, but no universal threshold automatically requires a split.

3. PROTECT BEHAVIOR BEFORE MOVING IT
- Identify public/API/CLI/schema/serialization/output/artifact behavior that must survive.
- Add or strengthen characterization/regression tests before risky movement when current coverage does not pin the behavior.
- Separate behavior changes from readability refactors. If a semantic repair is necessary, make its contract and proof explicit rather than hiding it inside cleanup.
- Never weaken tests, validators, types, schemas, or error handling merely to make extraction easier.

4. REFACTOR FOR COHESION, NOT SMALLNESS ALONE
- Give each module/class/function one coherent reason to change and one obvious owner.
- Keep related logic together; extract only when the new boundary has a meaningful name, contract, reuse point, test seam, or independent responsibility.
- Prefer direct control flow and domain-revealing names over cleverness. Flatten avoidable nesting with guard clauses or smaller coherent operations when that clarifies the path.
- Centralize duplicated deterministic rules in the existing canonical owner rather than inventing another helper family.
- Keep public surfaces narrow and dependencies explicit.
- Comments should preserve WHY, invariants, hazards, or non-obvious constraints; remove comments that merely narrate code or became stale.
- Remove proven dead code and obsolete compatibility shims only after checking callers/history/contracts.
- If a file is generated or derived, repair its canonical source/template/generator and regenerate it. Never hand-edit generated output for tidiness.

5. DO NOT REPLACE A MONOLITH WITH A MAZE
Reject refactors that create excessive tiny files, wrapper chains, pass-through classes, one-use abstractions, indirection without ownership value, generic utility dumping grounds, or dependency injection ceremony with no demonstrated seam. Local readability and cohesive proximity matter. A large function or module may remain when it is coherent, well-named, and safer to understand in one place.

6. ITERATE ON THE HIGHEST-VALUE HOTSPOT
Pass 1: implement the smallest behavior-preserving structural repair with targeted proof.
Pass 2: read the resulting diff from the perspective of a fresh maintainer and ask: where would I change this responsibility now; did the edit surface become more obvious; did extraction create new indirection, duplication, or scattered ownership; what high-impact structural debt remains? Repair concrete in-scope findings and rerun affected checks. Continue only while a practical evidenced readability gain remains; do not manufacture churn.

7. PROVE EDITABILITY, NOT JUST GREEN TESTS
Run formatter/linter/type/build/tests and repository validators appropriate to the touched code. Compare before/after structural signals when tools or simple measurements are available, but do not optimize a proxy alone. Include at least one representative maintenance question or edit path such as `Where would a fresh maintainer change <responsibility>?` and prove it resolves to a smaller or more obvious owner set without losing required context. Run `git diff --check` and inspect the final diff for behavior drift and needless movement.

SCOPE BOUNDARY
- P76 owns harness/spec progressive disclosure; P78 owns documentation diet; P63 owns skill factoring; P68 owns model-context engineering; P06 owns Git/PR cleanup. Use those owners when the primary defect lives there instead of absorbing their scope into this prompt.
- Do not combine unrelated feature work with readability cleanup merely because nearby code is ugly. If a broader cleanup is useful but not required for the bounded change, record and route it separately.

DELIVER
Report the structural-debt ledger, highest-impact repairs, files/functions/modules moved or simplified, preserved behavior/contracts, characterization/regression proof, before/after editability evidence, validation, commit/PR/merge/mainline state, remaining deferred debt, and the exact next executable action. Keep the closeout concise; the code should carry the readability improvement.
